lesson.title: Splitting the Difference Between Big States and Small
lesson.summary: The Great Compromise of July 1787 resolved the Constitutional Convention's deadlock over representation by creating a two-house Congress, one chamber based on population and one giving every state equal votes.
lesson.body:
The Constitutional Convention had reached a genuine impasse by the early summer of 1787. Delegates from large states like Virginia and Pennsylvania backed the Virginia Plan, which based representation in the national legislature on each state's population, reasoning that a state with more people and more wealth deserved a bigger voice. Delegates from small states like New Jersey and Delaware were alarmed, fearing that under such a system they would be permanently outvoted on every issue that mattered to them, and they rallied around the New Jersey Plan's insistence on equal representation for every state regardless of size.

Neither side would budge, and by late June the convention was in real danger of collapsing entirely without producing any new government at all. The breakthrough came from the Connecticut delegation, particularly Roger Sherman and Oliver Ellsworth, who proposed a solution that gave each side part of what it wanted rather than declaring one side the winner. Their plan called for a legislature with two separate chambers.

The lower chamber, the House of Representatives, would be apportioned by population, so that larger states like Virginia would send more representatives than smaller states like Delaware. The upper chamber, the Senate, would give every state exactly two seats regardless of population, ensuring that small states retained an equal voice on matters that came before that body. Because most legislation would need to pass both chambers, neither large states nor small states could simply dominate the other, and each side could point to at least one part of the new Congress built to protect its interests.

The convention adopted this arrangement, often called the Connecticut Compromise as well as the Great Compromise, on July 16, 1787, after a vote that was close enough to suggest just how fragile the agreement really was. Some large-state delegates, including a frustrated James Madison, worried privately that giving small states equal footing in the Senate was a step backward from the fully proportional government they had envisioned in the Virginia Plan. But most delegates recognized that without some concession along these lines, several small states were prepared to walk out of the convention altogether, which would have doomed the entire project of writing a new constitution.

The compromise's structure still shapes American government today, giving less populous states outsized influence in the Senate while keeping the House more directly responsive to population shifts. At the convention itself, resolving the representation question also cleared the way for delegates to turn to an equally difficult and morally fraught issue that had been lurking alongside it: how enslaved people, who could not vote or hold office, would be counted when determining each state's population for representation purposes.
